content.prompt: Consider the scores $2, 3, 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: A score of 23 is added to the dataset. How will this affect the IQR?

answer.worked:
Exclude the median when dividing the original nine scores into halves.
$$\begin{align*}Q_1&=\frac{3+4}{2}=3.5\\Q_3&=\frac{6+7}{2}=6.5\\\mathrm{IQR}&=6.5-3.5=3\end{align*}$$
After adding 23, the ordered scores are $2,3,4,5,5,5,6,7,8,23$. Each half contains five scores.
$$\begin{align*}Q_1&=4\\Q_3&=7\\\mathrm{IQR}&=7-4=3\end{align*}$$
The IQR remains 3.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence, describe why the IQR is more useful than the range when there are outliers.

answer.short: The range increases from 6 to 21, while the IQR remains 3. The IQR measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data and is less affected by outliers.

inlines.text: Which of the following statements is true for the people surveyed?
(A) The same percentage of people in each group earned more than $325 per week.
(B) Approximately 75% of people under 21 earned less than $350 per week.
(C) Approximately 75% of people 21 years and older earned more than $350 per week.
(D) Approximately 50% of people in each group earned between $325 and $350 per week.

answer.worked:
A: $\$325$ is the median for people under 21 and the lower quartile for people 21 years and older. Approximately $50\%$ and $75\%$, respectively, earned more than this amount, so A is false.

B: $\$350$ is the upper quartile for people under 21. Approximately $75\%$ earned less than this amount, so B is true.

C: $\$350$ is the upper quartile for people 21 years and older. Approximately $25\%$ earned more than this amount, so C is false.

D: For people under 21, $\$325$ to $\$350$ runs from the median to the upper quartile and contains approximately $25\%$ of the group, so D is false.

Correct answer: B.

answer.worked:
There are 50 scores, so the quartile positions are
$$\begin{aligned}Q_1\text{ position}&=0.25\times50=12.5\\Q_3\text{ position}&=0.75\times50=37.5.\end{aligned}$$
Only four scores are 15, so the 12th and 13th scores are at least 16: $Q_1\ge16$. The cumulative frequency at 18 is 40, so the 37th and 38th scores are at most 18: $Q_3\le18$.
Since $Q_3-Q_1=2$, these bounds force $Q_1=16$ and $Q_3=18$.
Both the 12th and 13th scores must therefore be 16. Hence at least 13 scores must be at most 16, giving $y\ge13$.
This is attainable with cumulative frequencies $y=13$ and $x=35$, for which the 37th and 38th scores are both 18. Therefore $y_{\min}=13$.

How many children aged 0–18 years are there in 2010?

answer.worked:
In 2010, $12$ years is the upper quartile, so ages 12–18 represent $25\%$ of the children. This is $875$ children.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Total}&=875\div0.25\\&=3500\end{aligned}$$
There were $3500$ children aged 0–18 years.

inlines.answer: 3 is an outlier, outside the range of 19–35.

answer.worked:
$Q_1=25$, $Q_3=29$.
$$\begin{aligned}IQR&=29-25=4\\\text{Lower fence}&=25-1.5\times4=19\\\text{Upper fence}&=29+1.5\times4=35\end{aligned}$$
$3<19$, so $3$ is the only outlier.

answer.worked:
$\begin{aligned}Q_1&=6,\quad Q_3=9\\\text{IQR}&=9-6=3\\\text{Lower fence}&=6-1.5\times3=1.5\\\text{Upper fence}&=9+1.5\times3=13.5\end{aligned}$

Since $1<1.5$, the only outlier is $1$.

answer.short: IQR $=5$; lower fence $=-7.5$; upper fence $=12.5$. No outliers.

All values lie between the fences, so there are no outliers.

inlines.text: The rainfall in mm for the past nine months was as follows:
Is the 31 an outlier for this dataset? Justify your answer with calculations.

answer.short: Yes. $Q_1=15.5$, $Q_3=21$, $\mathrm{IQR}=5.5$ and the upper fence is $29.25\text{ mm}$. Since $31>29.25$, $31\text{ mm}$ is an outlier.
answer.worked:
Ordered rainfall (mm): $14,15,16,17,19,20,20,22,31$. Excluding the median, $19$, from both halves:
$$\begin{align*}Q_1&=\frac{15+16}{2}=15.5\\Q_3&=\frac{20+22}{2}=21\\\mathrm{IQR}&=Q_3-Q_1\\&=21-15.5=5.5\\\text{Upper fence}&=Q_3+1.5\times\mathrm{IQR}\\&=21+1.5\times5.5\\&=29.25\text{ mm}\end{align*}$$
Since $31>29.25$, $31\text{ mm}$ is an outlier.

content.prompt:
In a small business, the seven employees earn the following wages per week:

$\$300$, $\$490$, $\$520$, $\$590$, $\$660$, $\$680$, $\$970$

children.label: a
children.prompt: Is the wage of $\$970$ an outlier for this set of data? Justify your answer with calculations.

answer.short: Yes. $\$970$ exceeds the upper fence of $\$965$.
answer.worked:
The wages are ordered: $300,490,520,590,660,680,970$. Excluding the median, $590$, the lower and upper halves give $Q_1=490$ and $Q_3=680$.

$$\begin{align*}\mathrm{IQR}&=Q_3-Q_1\\\mathrm{IQR}&=680-490\\\mathrm{IQR}&=190\end{align*}$$

To check for upper outliers:

$$\begin{align*}\text{Upper fence}&=Q_3+1.5\times\mathrm{IQR}\\\text{Upper fence}&=680+1.5(190)\\\text{Upper fence}&=680+285\\\text{Upper fence}&=965\end{align*}$$

Since $970>965$, the wage of $\$970$ is an outlier.

children.label: b
children.prompt:
Each employee receives a $\$20$ pay increase.

What effect will this have on the standard deviation?

answer.short: No effect. The spread does not change.
answer.worked: The standard deviation is unchanged. Adding $\$20$ to every wage also increases the mean by $\$20$, so each wage's deviation from the mean stays the same.

inlines.text: A set of data has a lower quartile (
What is the maximum possible range for this set of data if there are no outliers?

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}\mathrm{IQR} &= Q_U-Q_L\\\mathrm{IQR} &= 16-10\\\mathrm{IQR} &= 6\end{align*}$$
With no outliers, the minimum and maximum must lie within the outlier boundaries.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Lower bound} &= Q_L-1.5\times\mathrm{IQR}\\\text{Lower bound} &= 10-1.5(6)\\\text{Lower bound} &= 10-9\\\text{Lower bound} &= 1\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\text{Upper bound} &= Q_U+1.5\times\mathrm{IQR}\\\text{Upper bound} &= 16+1.5(6)\\\text{Upper bound} &= 16+9\\\text{Upper bound} &= 25\end{align*}$$
To maximise the range, the minimum can be $1$ and the maximum can be $25$. Values equal to the boundaries are not outliers.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Maximum range} &= 25-1\\\text{Maximum range} &= 24\end{align*}$$
The maximum possible range is $24$.

content.prompt: The interquartile range of a set of data is 10. If there are no outliers in this dataset, what is the largest possible range?

answer.worked:
Since $1.5\times\mathrm{IQR}=15$, all values lie within $[Q_1-15,\ Q_3+15]$. The largest possible range is the difference between these fences.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Maximum range} &= (Q_3+15)-(Q_1-15)\\\text{Maximum range} &= \mathrm{IQR}+30\\\text{Maximum range} &= 10+30=40\end{align*}$$

Under 21: minimum 200, lower quartile 250, median 325, upper quartile 350, maximum 450. entries.description:
Supplied blue worked answer:
- Option A: For "People under 21 years", 325 is the median (50% earned more). For "People 21 years and older", 325 is the lower quartile (75% earned more). This is false.
- Option B: For "People under 21 years", 350 is the upper quartile (Q₃). This means 75% of this group earned less than $350. This is true.
- Option C: For "People 21 years and older", 350 is the upper quartile. This means 25% earned more than $350, not 75%. This is false.
- Option D: For "People under 21 years", the range $325 to $350 is from Q₂ to Q₃ (25% of the group). This is false.
Therefore, Option B is the only true statement.

entries.description: Formal Definition of an Outlier

Source text: “Data values more than 1.5 times the IQR below Q₁ and above Q₃ is defined as an outlier.” Author corrected editable text: “A data value is an outlier if it is below Q₁ − 1.5 × IQR or above Q₃ + 1.5 × IQR. Values exactly on either fence are not outliers.”

Left- and right-directed arrows beneath the whiskers are each labelled 1.5 × IQR, extending from the corresponding quartile to a fence boundary. entries.description:
2017 HSC Standard 2 Band 5
A set of data has a lower quartile (Q_L) of 10 and an upper quartile (Q_U) of 16
What is the maximum possible range for this set of data if there are no outliers?

presentation.sourceReference: Quartiles and Box Plots, PDF version 261006, page 44, question 11
presentation.layout: Question number at left; source identity in bold above the stem. Substantial working space below.
presentation.notation: Preserve Q_L and Q_U as native mathematical subscripts.
presentation.answerPlacement: Supplied blue response becomes editable answer content, excluded from the student prompt.

entries.description:
First, find the interquartile range (IQR):
IQR = Q_U − Q_L
= 16 − 10
= 6

To have no outliers, the minimum and maximum data values must lie within the outlier boundaries.
Lower bound = Q_L − 1.5 × IQR
= 10 − 1.5(6)
= 10 − 9
= 1

Upper bound = Q_U + 1.5 × IQR
= 16 + 1.5(6)
= 16 + 9
= 25

To maximise the range without outliers, the minimum score can be 1 and the maximum score can be 25.
Maximum Range = 25 − 1
= 24

The maximum possible range is 24.
